# Deploy API gateway listeners in Kubernetes

This topic describes how to deploy Consul API gateway listeners to Kubernetes-orchestrated environments. If you want to implement API gateway listeners on VMs, refer to [Deploy API gateway listeners to virtual machines](/consul/docs/north-south/api-gateway/vm/listener).

## Overview

API gateways have one or more listeners that serve as ingress points for requests to services in a Consul service mesh. Create an [API gateway configuration](/consul/docs/reference/k8s/api-gateway/gateway) and define listeners that expose ports on the endpoint for ingress. Apply the configuration to direct Kubernetes to start API gateway services. 

### Routes

After deploying the gateway, attach HTTP or TCP [routes](/consul/docs/reference/k8s/api-gateway/routes) to listeners defined in the gateway to control how requests route to services in the network.

### Intentions

Configure Consul intentions to allow or prevent traffic between gateway listeners and services in the mesh. Refer to [Service intentions](/consul/docs/secure-mesh/intention) for additional information. 


## Requirements

1. Verify that your environment meets the requirements specified in [Technical specifications for Kubernetes](/consul/docs/north-south/api-gateway/k8s/tech-specs).
1. Verify that the Consul API gateway CRDs were applied. Refer to [Installation](/consul/docs/north-south/api-gateway/k8s/enable) for details.
1. If your Kubernetes-orchestrated network runs on OpenShift, verify that OpenShift is enabled for your Consul installation. Refer to [OpenShift requirements](/consul/docs/connect/gateways/api-gateway/tech-specs#openshift-requirements) for additional information. 

## Define the API gateways and listeners

Review [When to choose the Standard API gateway or Consul API gateway](/consul/docs/north-south/api-gateway/k8s#introduction) for guidance on selecting the right gateway type.

Create an API gateway values file that defines the gateway and listeners.

1. Specify the following fields:
    - `apiVersion`: Specifies the Kubernetes gateway API version. Must be `gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1` for Standard API gateway or `consul.hashicorp.com/v1beta1` for Consul API gateway. For more details on API version refer [Consul API gateway reference objects](/consul/docs/north-south/api-gateway/k8s#consul-api-gateway-reference-objects).
    - `kind`: Specifies the type of configuration entry to implement. This must be `Gateway`. 
    - `metadata.name`:  Specify a name for the gateway configuration. The name is metadata that you can use to reference the configuration when performing Consul operations.
    - `metadata.label.component`: Specify the component name as `api-gateway` for Standard API gateway or `api-gateway-consul` for Consul API gateway.
    - `spec.gatewayClassName`:  Specify the name of a `gatewayClass` object. Gateway classes are template-like resources in Kubernetes for instantiating gateway services. Specify `consul` for Standard API gateway or `consul-custom` for Consul API gateway to use the default gateway class shipped with Consul. Refer to the [GatewayClass configuration reference](/consul/docs/reference/k8s/api-gateway/gatewayclass) for additional information.
    - `spec.listeners`: Specify a list of listener configurations. Each listener is map containing the following fields:
      - `port`: Specifies the port that the listener receives traffic on.
      - `name`: Specifies a unique name for the listener.
      - `protocol`: You can set either `tcp` or `http` 
      - To serve HTTP/2 or gRPC traffic, add a listener protocol annotation to the `Gateway`. Refer to [HTTP/2 and gRPC listeners](#http-2-and-grpc-listeners) for additional information.
      - `allowedRoutes.namespaces`: Contains configurations for determining which namespaces are allowed to attach a route to the listener. 
2. Configure any additional fields necessary for your use case, such as the namespace or admin partition. Refer to the [API gateway configuration entry reference](/consul/docs/reference/k8s/api-gateway/gateway) for additional information.
3. Save the configuration.

In the following example, the API gateway specifies an HTTP listener on port `80`:

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: my-gateway
  namespace: consul
  labels:
    component: api-gateway
spec:
  gatewayClassName: consul
  listeners:
  - protocol: HTTP
    port: 80
    name: http
    allowedRoutes:
      namespaces:
        from: "All"
```


## Kubernetes SDS implementation

This section reflects the current API gateway SDS behavior in consul-k8s:

- Listener-level SDS from Gateway annotations and listener `tls.options`
- Backend-level SDS override from `RouteTLSSDSFilter`

### Listener SDS source of truth

Listener TLS SDS is resolved from these sources:

- Listener `tls.options` (per-listener override)
- Gateway `metadata.annotations` (gateway-wide defaults)

Supported keys:

- `api-gateway.consul.hashicorp.com/tls_sds_cluster_name`
- `api-gateway.consul.hashicorp.com/tls_sds_cert_resource`

### SDS resolution behavior

For each listener:

- If both SDS keys are set in listener `tls.options`, listener values are used.
- Otherwise, Gateway annotations are used as defaults.
- If neither source sets SDS, listener SDS is unset.

### Listener validation behavior

- If only one SDS field is provided, listener validation fails.
- SDS and `tls.certificateRefs` are validated independently and can both be configured on the same listener.

### Translation to Consul entries

- Resolved listener SDS is mapped to `APIGatewayListener.TLS.SDS`.
- Listener certificate refs are mapped to `APIGatewayListener.TLS.Certificates`.
- When both are configured, translated listener TLS includes both SDS and Certificates.

### Example: Gateway listener SDS via annotations and listener `tls.options`

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: sds-gateway
  namespace: default
  annotations:
    api-gateway.consul.hashicorp.com/tls_sds_cluster_name: sds-cluster
    api-gateway.consul.hashicorp.com/tls_sds_cert_resource: wildcard.ingress.consul
    labels:
    component: api-gateway
spec:
  gatewayClassName: consul
  listeners:
  - name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
    port: 8443
    hostname: a.example.test
    tls:
      mode: Terminate
      options:
        api-gateway.consul.hashicorp.com/tls_sds_cluster_name: sds-cluster
        api-gateway.consul.hashicorp.com/tls_sds_cert_resource: wil.ingr.consul
```

### TLS SDS precedence

Effective certificate selection precedence is:

1. Route service override `TLS.SDS`
1. Listener `TLS.SDS`
1. Gateway-level `TLS.SDS`

## Route service SDS overrides (Kubernetes)

`RouteTLSSDSFilter` remains the backend-level SDS override mechanism for HTTP routes.

- Kind: `RouteTLSSDSFilter`
- Spec fields:
  - `spec.sds.clusterName` (optional when inherited from listener/global SDS)
  - `spec.sds.certResource` (required)

Inheritance behavior:

- If `spec.sds.clusterName` is omitted, it is accepted when the route resolves exactly one listener-level SDS cluster from parentRefs.
- If inherited cluster resolution is missing or ambiguous, validation rejects the filter.

Usage pattern:

- Attach from `HTTPRoute.rules[].backendRefs[].filters[]` with `type: ExtensionRef`.
- Use `extensionRef.group: consul.hashicorp.com`.
- Use `extensionRef.kind: RouteTLSSDSFilter`.
- Use `extensionRef.name: <filter-name>`.

Validation and translation:

- Translation maps this to `HTTPService.TLS.SDS`.
- Missing filter object, wrong type, missing/empty `spec.sds.certResource`, or missing/ambiguous inherited `clusterName` are rejected.
- Rule-level placement (`HTTPRoute.rules[].filters[]`) is invalid for this override; backendRef filter placement is required.

### Example: HTTPRoute backendRef override using RouteTLSSDSFilter

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: api-route-override
  namespace: default
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: sds-gateway
    sectionName: https
  hostnames:
  - b.example.test
  rules:
  - backendRefs:
    - name: svc-b
      port: 5678
      filters:
      - type: ExtensionRef
        extensionRef:
          group: consul.hashicorp.com
          kind: RouteTLSSDSFilter
          name: route-sds-override-http
---
apiVersion: consul.hashicorp.com/v1alpha1
kind: RouteTLSSDSFilter
metadata:
  name: route-sds-override-http
  namespace: default
spec:
  sds:
    clusterName: sds-cluster-2
    certResource: foo.example.com
```

### Troubleshooting checklist

- Confirm both SDS keys are set together (listener `tls.options` or Gateway annotation defaults).
- If `tls.certificateRefs` are used, verify referenced Secrets exist and are referenceable.
- For backend overrides, ensure `RouteTLSSDSFilter` is attached under `backendRefs[].filters[]`.
- Ensure `RouteTLSSDSFilter.spec.sds.certResource` is non-empty and `clusterName` is set or inherited.
- Verify rendered config contains `APIGatewayListener.TLS.SDS`, `APIGatewayListener.TLS.Certificates`, and/or `HTTPService.TLS.SDS` as applicable.
- For local probes on non-8443 ports (for example `18443`), preserve hostname routing with `Host` and `--resolve`.

Refer to [Define API gateway routes in Kubernetes](/consul/docs/north-south/api-gateway/k8s/route), [RouteTLSSDSFilter reference (Kubernetes)](/consul/docs/north-south/api-gateway/k8s/routetlssdsfilter), and [Route Resource Configuration](/consul/docs/reference/k8s/api-gateway/routes) for route and filter configuration details.

## Deploy the API gateway and listeners

Apply the configuration to your cluster using the `kubectl` command. The following command applies the configuration to the `consul` namespace:

```shell-session
$ kubectl apply -f my-gateway.yaml -n consul
```
## Terminate HTTPS with Consul-managed certificates

You can configure the API gateway to terminate downstream HTTPS with its Consul service mesh leaf certificate instead of a certificate that you store in a Kubernetes `Secret`. Consul issues and rotates the leaf certificate automatically, so you do not need to create a `Secret` or configure `tls.certificateRefs` on the listener.

The leaf certificate is signed by the Consul service mesh certificate authority (CA) and includes wildcard DNS subject alternative names (SANs), such as `*.api-gateway.consul` and `*.api-gateway.<datacenter>.consul`. Consul also registers each service that a bound route targets in Consul DNS at `<service>.api-gateway.<domain>`. As a result, clients that trust the Consul CA root certificate can reach the service over verified HTTPS without additional certificate configuration. Refer to [Certificate DNS names](/consul/docs/north-south/api-gateway/secure-traffic/encrypt#certificate-dns-names) for the complete list of SANs, including the namespace-scoped SANs for Consul Enterprise.

### Requirements for Consul-managed certificates

- Consul v2.1 or later
- Consul Helm chart v2.1.0 or later
- To resolve `<service>.api-gateway.<domain>` names from pods, enable Consul DNS with the [`dns.enabled`](/consul/docs/reference/k8s/helm#v-dns-enabled) Helm value and configure your cluster DNS to forward the `consul` domain to Consul. Refer to [Resolve Consul DNS requests in Kubernetes](/consul/docs/discover/dns/k8s) for instructions.

### Enable Consul-managed TLS on the gateway

Add the `consul.hashicorp.com/tls-enabled: "true"` annotation to the `Gateway` resource and configure an `HTTPS` listener without `tls.certificateRefs`. Consul on Kubernetes translates the annotation into the [`TLS.Enabled`](/consul/docs/reference/config-entry/api-gateway#tls-enabled) field of the API gateway configuration entry. The annotation is supported on both the Standard API gateway (`gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1`) and the Consul API gateway (`consul.hashicorp.com/v1beta1`).

The following example configures an `HTTPS` listener on port `8443`:

<CodeBlockConfig filename="my-gateway.yaml" highlight="5-6,15-18">

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: my-gateway
  annotations:
    consul.hashicorp.com/tls-enabled: "true"
  labels:
    component: api-gateway
spec:
  gatewayClassName: consul
  listeners:
  - name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
    port: 8443
    tls:
      mode: Terminate
      options:
        api-gateway.consul.hashicorp.com/tls_min_version: "TLS_AUTO"
    allowedRoutes:
      namespaces:
        from: "All"
```

</CodeBlockConfig>

Kubernetes Gateway API v1.4 and later CRDs require a `Terminate` listener to set either `tls.certificateRefs` or `tls.options`. When you omit `tls.certificateRefs`, set a `tls.options` key, such as `api-gateway.consul.hashicorp.com/tls_min_version: "TLS_AUTO"`, to satisfy the validation rule. The `TLS_AUTO` value does not change the gateway's TLS behavior.

Bind an `HTTPRoute` to the listener and create service intentions that allow traffic from the gateway to the destination service. The following example routes traffic to the `static-server` service:

<CodeBlockConfig filename="my-route.yaml">

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: my-route
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: my-gateway
  rules:
  - backendRefs:
    - name: static-server
      port: 80
```

</CodeBlockConfig>

Apply the configurations to your cluster:

```shell-session
$ kubectl apply --filename my-gateway.yaml --filename my-route.yaml
```

Certificates that you configure on a listener with `tls.certificateRefs` or SDS take precedence for requests whose server name indication (SNI) matches the certificate hosts. The leaf certificate serves all other requests. When you remove the annotation, Consul sets `TLS.Enabled` to `false` in the API gateway configuration entry.

### Verify DNS resolution

When the `HTTPRoute` binds to the gateway, Consul maps each service that the route targets to the gateway in the gateway-services catalog mapping, which is the same mapping that ingress gateways use. Consul resolves `<service>.api-gateway.<domain>` queries from this mapping. Refer to [API gateway service mapping](/consul/docs/discover/service/static#api-gateway-service-mapping) for more information.

Complete the following steps to verify the mapping and DNS resolution:

1. Confirm that Consul mapped the service to the gateway. The gateway name in the mapping is the name of the `Gateway` resource. If ACLs are enabled, set `CONSUL_HTTP_TOKEN` to a token with `service:read` permission on the gateway. The following example assumes that you installed Consul in the `consul` namespace with [`global.tls.enabled`](/consul/docs/reference/k8s/helm#v-global-tls-enabled) set to `true`.

   ```shell-session
   $ kubectl exec --namespace consul consul-server-0 -- \
       curl --silent --cacert /consul/tls/ca/tls.crt \
       --header "X-Consul-Token: $CONSUL_HTTP_TOKEN" \
       https://localhost:8501/v1/catalog/gateway-services/my-gateway \
       | jq '[.[] | {Service: .Service.Name, GatewayKind, Port}]'
   ```

   The output includes an entry for the service with `"GatewayKind": "api-gateway"` and the listener port:

   ```json
   [
     {
       "Service": "static-server",
       "GatewayKind": "api-gateway",
       "Port": 8443
     }
   ]
   ```

1. Resolve the service name from a pod in the cluster. The A record returns the address of each healthy gateway instance, and the SRV record returns the listener port.

   ```shell-session
   $ kubectl run dns-test --rm --stdin --restart=Never --image=anubhavmishra/tiny-tools -- \
       dig +short static-server.api-gateway.consul A static-server.api-gateway.consul SRV
   ```

   If the lookup does not return any records, verify that the `HTTPRoute` status shows that the route is accepted and bound to the gateway, and that your cluster DNS forwards the `consul` domain to Consul DNS. Refer to [Verify API gateway DNS resolution](/consul/docs/discover/service/static#verify-api-gateway-dns-resolution) for additional troubleshooting steps.

### Verify HTTPS traffic

Complete the following steps to verify that the gateway terminates HTTPS with a certificate that clients can trust:

1. Retrieve the active Consul service mesh CA root certificate from a Consul server. The following example assumes that you installed Consul in the `consul` namespace with [`global.tls.enabled`](/consul/docs/reference/k8s/helm#v-global-tls-enabled) set to `true`. If TLS is not enabled, use `http://localhost:8500` instead.

   ```shell-session
   $ kubectl exec --namespace consul consul-server-0 -- \
       curl --silent --cacert /consul/tls/ca/tls.crt https://localhost:8501/v1/connect/ca/roots \
       | jq --raw-output '.Roots[] | select(.Active) | .RootCert' > consul-ca.pem
   ```

1. Copy the CA root certificate to a client pod that can resolve Consul DNS. Replace `CLIENT_POD` with the name of the pod.

   ```shell-session
   $ kubectl cp consul-ca.pem CLIENT_POD:/tmp/consul-ca.pem
   ```

1. Send an HTTPS request to the service through the gateway and verify the certificate with the CA root certificate:

   ```shell-session
   $ kubectl exec CLIENT_POD -- curl --cacert /tmp/consul-ca.pem https://static-server.api-gateway.consul:8443
   ```

   The request succeeds without the `--insecure` flag because the gateway certificate includes the `*.api-gateway.consul` SAN and chains to the Consul service mesh CA.

In Consul Enterprise, when you enable [Kubernetes namespace mirroring](/consul/docs/reference/k8s/helm#v-connectinject-consulnamespaces-mirroringk8s), services in a non-default namespace use namespace-scoped SANs, such as `*.api-gateway.<namespace>.consul`. To verify the gateway certificate, clients must send a server name that matches these SANs, for example `static-server.api-gateway.<namespace>.consul`.

## HTTP/2 and gRPC listeners

By default, Consul on Kubernetes configures `HTTP` and `HTTPS` listeners to use HTTP/1.1 for the connection from the gateway to the backend service. To serve HTTP/2 or gRPC traffic from the client to the backend service, add the `api-gateway.consul.hashicorp.com/listener-<sectionName>-protocol` annotation to the `Gateway`. Replace `<sectionName>` with the name of the listener and set the value to `http2` or `grpc`. Each listener reads only its own annotation, so listeners on the same `Gateway` can use different protocols.

### Requirements for HTTP/2 and gRPC listeners

- Consul v2.1 or later
- Consul Helm chart v2.1.0 or later
- A `Gateway` and `HTTPRoute` in the `gateway.networking.k8s.io` API group

### Configure HTTP/2 and gRPC listeners

Complete the following steps to route HTTP/2 and gRPC traffic through an API gateway:

1. Set the protocol of each backend service in a `ServiceDefaults` resource. The following example sets the `grpc-server` protocol to `grpc` and the `h2-server` protocol to `http2`:

   <CodeBlockConfig filename="servicedefaults.yaml">

   ```yaml
   apiVersion: consul.hashicorp.com/v1alpha1
   kind: ServiceDefaults
   metadata:
     name: grpc-server
   spec:
     protocol: grpc
   ---
   apiVersion: consul.hashicorp.com/v1alpha1
   kind: ServiceDefaults
   metadata:
     name: h2-server
   spec:
     protocol: http2
   ```

   </CodeBlockConfig>

1. Define the `Gateway` with a listener for each protocol, and add a protocol annotation for each `http2` or `grpc` listener. Set the listener `protocol` field to `HTTP` or `HTTPS`:

   <CodeBlockConfig filename="my-gateway.yaml" highlight="5-7">

   ```yaml
   apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
   kind: Gateway
   metadata:
     name: my-gateway
     annotations:
       api-gateway.consul.hashicorp.com/listener-grpc-listener-protocol: "grpc"
       api-gateway.consul.hashicorp.com/listener-h2-listener-protocol: "http2"
   spec:
     gatewayClassName: consul
     listeners:
     - name: http-listener
       protocol: HTTP
       port: 80
       allowedRoutes:
         namespaces:
           from: All
     - name: grpc-listener
       protocol: HTTP
       port: 9080
       allowedRoutes:
         namespaces:
           from: All
     - name: h2-listener
       protocol: HTTP
       port: 9090
       allowedRoutes:
         namespaces:
           from: All
   ```

   </CodeBlockConfig>

   The `http-listener` listener does not have an annotation, so it uses the `http` protocol.

1. Bind an `HTTPRoute` to each listener with the `sectionName` field. The following example routes traffic from the `grpc-listener` listener to the `grpc-server` service:

   <CodeBlockConfig filename="grpc-route.yaml">

   ```yaml
   apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
   kind: HTTPRoute
   metadata:
     name: grpc-route
   spec:
     parentRefs:
     - name: my-gateway
       sectionName: grpc-listener
     rules:
     - backendRefs:
       - name: grpc-server
         port: 9000
   ```

   </CodeBlockConfig>

1. Apply the configurations:

   ```shell-session
   $ kubectl apply --filename servicedefaults.yaml --filename my-gateway.yaml --filename grpc-route.yaml
   ```

You can add, change, or remove the annotation on an existing `Gateway`. Consul on Kubernetes updates the listener protocol in the API gateway configuration entry and does not change the other listeners.

Consul on Kubernetes ignores an annotation value that is not `http`, `http2`, `grpc`, or `tcp`, and uses the protocol derived from the listener `protocol` field. When the `<sectionName>` in the annotation key does not match the name of any listener, the controller logs a warning that lists the ignored annotation keys.

### Verify HTTP/2 and gRPC listeners

Complete the following steps to verify that the gateway uses the configured protocols:

1. Read the API gateway configuration entry to confirm that each listener has the expected `Protocol` value. Run the command from a host where the `consul` CLI can reach your Consul servers, and set `CONSUL_HTTP_TOKEN` if ACLs are enabled.

   ```shell-session
   $ consul config read -kind api-gateway -name my-gateway
   ```

1. Forward the Envoy admin port of the gateway pod to your local machine:

   ```shell-session
   $ kubectl port-forward \
       $(kubectl get pods --selector gateway.consul.hashicorp.com/name=my-gateway --output jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') \
       19000:19000
   ```

1. In a separate terminal, confirm that the upstream cluster for the `grpc-server` service uses HTTP/2. The output includes `http2_protocol_options`:

   ```shell-session
   $ curl --silent localhost:19000/config_dump \
       | jq '.configs[]
         | select(."@type" | contains("ClustersConfigDump"))
         | .dynamic_active_clusters[]
         | select(.cluster.name | startswith("grpc-server."))
         | .cluster.typed_extension_protocol_options'
   ```

   Run the same command for the `h2-server` cluster. Upstream clusters for services that you route through an `http` listener do not include `http2_protocol_options`.

1. List the HTTP filters on each gateway listener. The listener for the `grpc-listener` listener includes the `grpc_stats` and `grpc_http1_bridge` HTTP filters:

   ```shell-session
   $ curl --silent localhost:19000/config_dump \
       | jq '.configs[]
         | select(."@type" | contains("ListenersConfigDump"))
         | .dynamic_listeners[]
         | {name: .name, filters: [.active_state.listener.filter_chains[].filters[].typed_config.http_filters[]?.name]}'
   ```
